LETTERS TO THE EDITOR

# Letter: The intersection of CHIP and HIV: Implications for cardiovascular risk stratification

To the Editor: We read with interest the article by Oren and colleagues1 highlighting the association between clonal hematopoiesis of indeterminate potential (CHIP) and increased cardiovascular risk and its rel­ evance to internal medicine practice. Expanding this discussion, we would like to describe the interactions between CHIP and human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection and their implications for internal medicine practice in settings where internists with HIV training often serve as primary care clinicians for people with HIV. People with HIV experience disproportionately high cardiovascular risk driven by chronic immune activation, persistent inflammation, antiretroviral therapy–associated metabolic effects, higher smoking prevalence, and traditional atherosclerotic risk fac­ tors. Emerging evidence suggests that CHIP is about twice as prevalent in people with HIV compared with HIV-negative individuals and may further amplify this risk burden.2 CHIP, particularly involving TET2 and DNMT3A mutations, contributes to clonal expansion of proinflammatory myeloid cells and activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome pathway, increasing interleu­ kin-1beta and interleukin-6 signaling and accelerating atherosclerosis, myocardial infarction risk, and mortal­ ity.2,3 CHIP also confers increased risk of hematologic malignancy, compounding long-term morbidity in this aging population. Thus, there is a need for dedicated screening and optimal treatment interventions.2,3 REPRIEVE (Randomized Trial to Prevent Vascu­ lar Events in HIV)2 demonstrated that pitavastatin reduces major adverse cardiovascular events in in­ dividuals with HIV with low-to-moderate tradition­ al risk, reinforcing the importance of early preven­ tive strategies. Although CHIP was not assessed in REPRIEVE, these findings raise the possibility that unmeasured inflammatory drivers such as CHIP may help identify patients who could benefit from earlier or more intensive intervention. CHIP remains underrecognized in HIV care, par­ ticularly among infectious diseases physicians who fre­ quently provide primary care for people with HIV. We agree with Oren and colleagues1 that comprehensive cardiovascular risk assessment is essential and propose CHIP as an emerging risk modifier in people with HIV.

Prospective studies are needed to guide screening and targeted interventions in this population.

In Reply: We thank Dr. Martinez and colleagues for their comment on the intersection between clonal hematopoiesis of indeterminate potential (CHIP) and cardiovascular risk in people with human immu­ nodeficiency virus (HIV) infection. We would like to shed light on recent data that may further inform this discussion. Since the REPRIEVE (Randomized Trial to Pre­ vent Vascular Events in HIV) trial was completed, Xue et al1 reported the results of a dedicated CHIP analy­ sis in 4,490 REPRIEVE participants using high-depth targeted sequencing. While CHIP overall was not associated with major adverse cardiovascular events, larger CHIP clones (variant allele fraction ≥ 10%) were associated with substantially higher odds of major adverse cardiovascular events, myocardial infarction, and coronary revascularization.1 Intriguingly, these as­ sociations persisted despite pitavastatin therapy, sug­ gesting that a component of residual cardiovascular risk in people with HIV may be driven by mechanisms beyond reductions in low-density lipoprotein choles­ terol, potentially involving NLRP3 inflammasome activation and downstream interleukin-1beta and interleukin-6 signaling.

These findings have broader implications across chronic inflammatory disorders. Conditions such as rheumatoid arthritis, antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody–associated vasculitis, gout, and VEXAS (vac­ uoles, E1 enzyme, X-linked, autoinflammatory, somat­ ic) syndrome are characterized by excess cardiovascular risk that is not fully explained by traditional risk factors, and have also been associated with increased preva­ lence of CHIP (see supplementary Figure 1 in the PDF version of this article).2–5 Chronic inflammatory signal­ ing may promote clonal expansion, while CHIP-asso­ ciated clones further amplify inflammation, creating a potentially self-reinforcing cycle and contributing to accelerated atherogenesis and the development of in­ flammatory cardiac conditions. In this context, CHIP may not only serve as a biomarker of cardiovascular risk but also as a tool for identifying patients most likely to benefit from approved and emerging anti-inflammatory therapies (supplementary Figure 1). Prospective studies in­ corporating CHIP assessment into cohorts of persons with HIV infection and other inflammatory disease will be important to accurately define its role in risk stratification, therapeutic selection, and precision cardiovascular prevention. The results of ongoing phase 3 trials evaluating interleukin-6 inhibition (ie, ZEUS [Effects of Ziltivekimab Versus Placebo on Cardiovascular Outcomes in Participants With Established Atherosclerotic Cardiovascular Disease, Chronic Kidney Disease and Systemic Inflammation] and ARTEMIS [Effects of Ziltivekimab Versus Pla­ cebo on Cardiovascular Outcomes in Patients With Acute Myocardial Infarction]) may help define the role of targeted anti-inflammatory therapy in preci­ sion cardiovascular prevention.

# Minding the Gap

**Authors:** Ohad Oren; Abhay Singh; Hetty E. Carraway; Venu Menon

**Affiliations:** aDepartment of Cardiovascular Medicine, Heart, Vascular, and Thoracic Institute, Cleveland Clinic Foundation, Cleveland, Ohio, USA | bLeukemia Program, Taussig Cancer Institute, Cleveland Clinic, Cleveland, Ohio, USA

Each year, hundreds of thousands of patients undergo genomic sequencing of blood or bone marrow samples during the evaluation of unexplained cytopenias; suspected hematologic malignancies; or as part of cancer diagnosis, treatment, and survivorship care.1 Across these clinical settings, approximately 10% to 30% of patients are found to harbor somatic mutations in hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells, many involving pathogenic variants associated with an increased risk of cardiovascular disease and/or increased risk for hematological malignancy.2 When these mutations are detected at a variant allele frequency (VAF) of at least 2%, a threshold used to define the proportion of sequencing reads containing the variant allele, they are categorized as clonal hematopoiesis of indeterminate potential (CHIP) in the absence of unexplained cytopenias or hematologic malignancy, or as clonal cytopenia of undetermined significance (CCUS) when persistent unexplained cytopenias are present.2 Although these findings are generally managed by hematologists, a growing body of evidence has established that many of these pathogenic variants also carry important cardiovascular implications, including significantly elevated risks of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, heart failure, arrhythmia, and venous thrombosis.3 Many of these patients continue to remain exclusively under the care of our hematology and oncology colleagues, representing a major missed opportunity for cardiovascular risk assessment and prevention. A practical referral pathway is outlined for high-risk patients, including those with large CHIP/CCUS (VAF >10%), CHIP/CCUS with TET2, TP53, or PPM1D mutations (VAF ≥2%), or JAK2 mutations (VAF ≥1%). CHIP and CCUS represent acquired processes in which hematopoietic stem cells and precursors accumulate mutations through repeated replication cycles, accelerated by mutagenic exposures (ie, tobacco, cytotoxic chemotherapy, radiation, etc) and germline vulnerabilities in DNA repair pathways.4 Pathogenic variants in genes governing DNA methylation (ie, DNMT3A, TET2), signal transduction (ie, JAK2), epigenetic regulation (ie, ASXL1), and RNA splicing (ie, SF3B1, SRSF2) may confer selective advantages to mutant hematopoietic stem cells, culminating in the generation of expanded clones with distinct, gene-specific biologic properties, including myeloid lineage bias, proinflammatory reprogramming of myeloid effector cells, and enhanced platelet activation. Because somatic mutations are acquired over the lifespan through repeated hematopoietic stem cell replication, the prevalence of CHIP/CCUS is strongly age-dependent: it is rare before age 40, detectable in approximately 10% of individuals over 70 years of age, and approaches 20% among nonagenarians.2 However, with sufficiently sensitive deep sequencing, small clonal populations may be nearly ubiquitous with aging.5 Driven by population aging, broader adoption of next-generation sequencing , and increasingly sensitive sequencing platforms capable of detecting clones with variant allele frequencies as low as 0.1%, the number of patients identified with somatic mutations in leukemia-associated genes is expected to rise substantially over the coming years.

The clinical consequences of CHIP/CCUS are diverse. First, they predispose to the development of myeloid and lymphoid malignancies at a rate of 0.5% to 1.0% per year.2, 6 Second, they substantially increase the risk of cardiovascular disease, which accounts for a significant proportion of the excess mortality observed in these populations.7 The cardiovascular implications of CHIP are gene-specific with TET2 and JAK2 variants exhibiting the strongest and most consistent associations with future manifest atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, with HRs of 1.9 and up to 12-fold, respectively.2, 7 In contrast, mutations in DNA damage repair genes (TP53 and PPM1D) have been associated with a broader spectrum of adverse cardiovascular outcomes, including coronary heart disease, incident peripheral artery disease, and markedly increased all-cause mortality (HR: 2.78).7 Notably, the excess cardiovascular risk associated with CHIP, particularly high-risk genotypes such as TET2, JAK2, and TP53, is of a magnitude comparable to or greater than that of traditional cardiovascular risk factors, including type 2 diabetes and hypertension. Several expert groups have accordingly proposed that CHIP be considered a risk-enhancing factor, warranting aggressive optimization of modifiable risk factors, including lipids, blood pressure, and glycemic index, as well as nicotine avoidance and weight reduction, through both lifestyle interventions and pharmacotherapy.8 A 2026 American Heart Association Scientific Statement on CHIP and cardiovascular disease further endorsed individualized cardiovascular risk assessment and primary and secondary prevention in the management of patients with CHIP/CCUS.9 Building on the growing evidence linking CHIP to cardiovascular disease, we propose and have adopted a multidisciplinary referral pathway to standardize cardiovascular evaluation after the detection of CHIP/CCUS. The immediate priority is to ensure that patients harboring high-risk somatic mutations receive comprehensive cardiovascular risk assessment and management of conventional cardiovascular risk factors and consideration of enrollment in clinical trials while mutation-specific therapies await validation in prospective clinical trials.

Our structured referral framework is presented in Figure 1. When whole-genome sequencing or targeted sequencing of blood or bone marrow specimens identifies pathogenic variants in cardiovascular-relevant genes (eg, TET2, TP53, PPM1D) at a VAF ≥2% (or ≥1% for JAK2) or large CHIP/CCUS (VAF>10%), the managing hematologist or oncologist should consider referral for cardiovascular evaluation. Ideally, patients should be evaluated by a dedicated CHIP cardiovascular specialist, where available, or alternatively by a cardio-oncologist or preventive cardiologist with expertise in clonal hematopoiesis. Close collaboration between hematology/oncology and cardiovascular medicine is essential to ensure that cardiovascular evaluation is tailored to the patient's hematologic and oncologic context, including the underlying diagnosis, distinction between somatic and germline variants when relevant, and ongoing or planned cardiotoxic therapies that may influence cardiovascular management or necessitate coordinated clinical decision-making.

The cardiovascular evaluation should follow previously proposed practical approaches for the management of patients with CHIP/CCUS and include a comprehensive assessment of traditional cardiovascular risk factors,8, 9 including smoking status, family history of premature atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, body mass index, blood pressure, lipid profile, and hemoglobin A1c. Existing imaging obtained as part of oncologic care should also be reviewed opportunistically for findings that may refine cardiovascular risk assessment, such as coronary artery calcification on chest computed tomography or breast arterial calcifications on mammogram. Echocardiography, including assessment of global longitudinal strain when appropriate, should be considered in patients with heart failure symptoms or those anticipated to receive potentially cardiotoxic therapies. In the absence of evidence, we do not advocate routine rhythm monitoring solely based on the presence of CHIP. In selected patients, however, a lower threshold for ambulatory monitoring may be reasonable, particularly with TET2 or JAK2 mutations given their associations with atrial fibrillation. Management should emphasize individualized, mutation-informed intensification of primary and secondary cardiovascular prevention in accordance with contemporary practical guidance, within a multidisciplinary care model involving hematology, oncology (when applicable), genetics, and cardiovascular medicine.8, 9

It is important to note that no prospective study has demonstrated that identification of CHIP followed by implementation of cardiovascular risk reduction strategies improves clinical outcomes compared with standard care. The proposed framework is therefore based on biological plausibility, observational evidence, and extrapolation from established cardiovascular prevention principles rather than prospective or randomized trial data. In addition, the optimal frequency of cardiovascular assessments and the cost-effectiveness of systematic referral remain undefined. This also underscores the importance of considering enrollment in available clinical trials and educating patients about such opportunities.

The alternative is difficult to justify: patients with mutations associated with substantial cardiovascular risk are currently identified without any standardized pathway for cardiovascular evaluation. The convergence of expanding next-generation sequencing utilization, a growing evidence base linking specific mutations to cardiovascular risk, and a broadening cardiometabolic therapeutic toolkit creates both the opportunity and the obligation to bridge the gap between hematologic detection and cardiovascular evaluation and management. Prospective registries and pragmatic trials evaluating the impact of structured cardiovascular referral pathways on clinical outcomes in patients with CHIP/CCUS are needed. In the interim, the framework proposed here offers a practical starting point for ensuring that the cardiovascular implications of CHIP/CCUS are no longer overlooked.

Ongoing clinical trials are evaluating targeted therapies for CHIP.

Clonal hematopoiesis of indeterminate potential (CHIP) is a preleukemic state in which a hematopoietic stem cell acquires a single leukemia driver mutation, resulting in clonal expansion.1 CHIP may be detected during the evaluation of unexplained blood count abnormalities or through germline testing in relatives of individuals with cancer. Furthermore, as cancer-directed therapies can induce genotoxic effects and promote clonal selection, people with or who have had cancer may manifest CHIP. Although CHIP confers an increased incidence of hematologic malignancies, most of the excess mortality results from cardiovascular disease.2,3

This primer reviews our approach to the cardiovascular assessment and care of individuals with CHIP using a clinical case.

## Clinical Case

A 59-year-old man with essential hypertension, diet-controlled type 2 diabetes mellitus, dyslipidemia, deep venous thrombosis, and localized melanoma was referred to the CHIP clinic because of a finding of BRAF, PLCG2, and TET2 CHIP during work-up for asymptomatic blood count abnormalities. Three months before referral, the patient had mild thrombocytosis (platelet count 501 × 109/L). His hemogram otherwise showed a hemoglobin concentration of 14.0 g/dL and a leukocyte count of 9 × 103/μL. Next-generation sequencing (NEBNext kit, New England Biolabs) detected pathogenic mutations involving TET2 (c.3581C>G) (variant allele fraction [VAF] 5.6%), BRAF (p.L597R) (VAF 4.1%), and PLCG2 (p.A708T) (VAF 2.8%).

The patient had localized melanoma of the shoulder 11 years prior requiring surgical excision. He led an active lifestyle and was a lifelong nonsmoker. He reported consuming 5 alcoholic drinks per week. His family history was notable for myocardial infarction in a paternal grandfather (in his 60s). His medications included aspirin 81 mg/d, atorvastatin 40 mg/d, lisinopril 2.5 mg/d, and apixaban 2.5 mg twice daily. Physical examination showed a heart rate of 68 beats/min, blood pressure of 112/74 mm Hg, weight of 98.1 kg, and a body mass index of 30.2 kg/m2. Twelve-lead electrocardiography demonstrated sinus rhythm. Laboratory work-up revealed a total cholesterol concentration of 139 mg/dL, a low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C) concentration of 88 mg/dL, a high-density lipoprotein cholesterol concentration of 29 mg/dL, a triglyceride concentration of 111 mg/dL, and glycated hemoglobin of 6.1%.

## The Biological and Clinical Cardiovascular Implications of CHIP

With age, hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells acquire somatic mutations. The vast majority of these are silent, but those in a handful of known leukemia driver genes promote expansion of the mutant clone. If a clone acquires additional mutations (usually ≥2 more), progression to hematologic malignancy may ensue. An arbitrary cutpoint defines CHIP as the presence of a somatic mutation in a leukemia driver gene involving at least 2% of peripheral leukocytes in the absence of overt hematological disease, cytopenia, or morphologic dysplasia. Of note, CHIP represents one subgroup among the broader spectrum of clonal hematopoiesis, which also encompasses other forms of somatic mosaicism characterized by structural chromosomal alterations rather than the presence of a leukemia driver mutation.

CHIP rarely affects individuals younger than 40 years and occurs in as many as 11.7% among those 80 to 89 years of age.1 CHIP may occur “de novo” or following cytotoxic anticancer therapies. The most commonly mutated driver genes in “de novo” cases, including in patients with cancer, are DNMT3A, TET2, and ASXL1, which encode epigenetic regulators with roles in hypo- and hypermethylation.1 In contrast, therapy-related CHIP associates more commonly with recurrent mutations in TP53, PPM1D, and ATM, genes with key functions in DNA damage and repair response (DDR). Whether germline factors predispose to CHIP has not been elucidated, although DDR and telomere maintenance genes may play a role. Although CHIP is associated with an increased risk for hematologic malignancy, the absolute risk (annual incidence ∼ 0.5%-1%) does not account for the elevated mortality rates. Atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD) predominates as a contributor to that gap, with relative risks for coronary artery disease and myocardial infarction between 2 and 4 for CHIP carriers compared with those without CHIP, independent of conventional cardiovascular risk factors.1,2

Several investigations have established a causal link between certain forms of CHIP and inflammasome-driven atherosclerosis. In mice, bone marrow reconstitution with TET2-deficient cells increases atherosclerotic plaque size, an effect mediated by NLPR3 inflammasome activation and downstream increases in interleukin (IL)–1β and IL-6 expression.2,4 Additional evidence for the association among TET2 CHIP, inflammation, and coronary artery disease comes from an exploratory analysis of CANTOS (Canakinumab Antiinflammatory Thrombosis Outcome Study), in which patients with TET2 CHIP had reduced major adverse cardiovascular event rates when treated with a monoclonal antibody neutralizing IL-1β. In murine models of Jak2 V617F CHIP, activation of the AIM2 inflammasome contributed to development of atherosclerotic lesions and neutrophil extracellular traps, implicated in venous thrombosis.5 A UK Biobank analysis revealed strong associations between the presence of JAK2 mutations and both prevalent and incident venous thromboembolic risk.6 In experimental studies of aberrant DDR genes recapitulating TP53 and PPM1D CHIP, macrophage proliferation was increased in arterial plaques with consequent expansion in peripheral artery plaque.7

## How Do We Integrate CHIP Data Into Cardiovascular Risk Assessment?

Studies have demonstrated an independent association between CHIP and a higher incidence of ischemic cardiovascular events, with significant effect sizes in TET2 and JAK2 CHIP, especially with large (VAF > 10%) clones (Figure 1).1,2 Mechanistically, NLRP3 and AIM2 inflammasomes have been implicated in atherogenesis and thrombogenesis in Tet2 and Jak2 CHIP, respectively. Analyses have demonstrated that TET2 CHIP and JAK2 CHIP are associated with approximately 2- and 12-fold increases in ischemic cardiovascular events, including myocardial infarction and stroke,2 conferring excess cardiovascular risk that resembles the magnitude of traditional cardiovascular risk factors.8 In addition, CHIP, in particular TET2 and PPM1D CHIP, independently potentiate the risk for ASCVD and mortality in patients who have had ischemic cardiac or cerebrovascular events. ## How Do We Approach Cardiovascular Prevention in Individuals With CHIP?

Given the current dearth of clinical trial evidence regarding management of CHIP, we can offer only our informed opinions at present. We do not screen for CHIP in unselected patients with cardiovascular disease, and many of our patients derive from our hematology and medical oncology colleagues following the detection of CHIP. Our CHIP clinic educates individuals and families about the nature of CHIP and the increased risk for ischemic cardiovascular and cerebrovascular events in particular subgroups, while acknowledging the evolving understanding of the associations.9 We provide a “patient page” of information for patients, their family members, and primary care physicians who may not have previously encountered CHIP.9 We stress the importance of maintaining healthy lifestyle habits in all patients, encouraging physical activity, the consumption of a healthy diet, and avoidance of smoking, vaping, and other nicotine products. In the absence of clinical trial evidence, we practice aggressive preventive cardiology and consider TET2, JAK2, PPM1D, and TP53 CHIP as secondary prevention equivalents and target lipid (LDL-C < 70 mg/dL), blood pressure (<130/80 mm Hg), and glycemic (glycated hemoglobin <6.5%) control (Figure 2). In individuals with large (VAF > 10%) TET2 or JAK2 CHIP, multiple TET2 CHIP, concomitant large TET2 and JAK2 mutations, or TET2 CHIP with elevated lipoprotein(a), which we consider particularly high risk, we strictly control lipids (LDL-C < 55 mg/dL) and blood pressure (<120/80 mm Hg).Figure 2Our Approach to Primary Prevention in Individuals With CHIPWe incorporate data on somatic mutation and clone size to devise a cardioprotective strategy. In individuals with JAK2 CHIP, we also engage in shared decision making regarding the utility and risks of primary prevention with low-dose aspirin, for which we have a low threshold in people at low bleeding risk who have coronary artery disease, history of venous thromboembolism, or strong family history of ASCVD. In patients with TET2 or JAK2 CHIP with history of ASCVD, we intensify secondary prevention efforts, attempting to achieve the lowest reasonable LDL-C level, often using multiple lipid-lowering agents, including statins, ezetimibe, and proprotein convertase subtilisin/kexin type 9 inhibitors, and we discuss with patients the addition of inclisiran or bempedoic acid on an individual basis. In persons with TET2 CHIP, we discuss empirical supplementation with vitamin C, a cofactor for the enzyme TET2, given preliminary evidence that it ameliorates DNA demethylation secondary to TET2 loss of function, although the optimal form and dose of vitamin C are unknown.10 In individuals with mutations in DDR genes, such as PPM1D and TP53, we pay special attention to arterial bruits, pedal pulses, and ankle-brachial index on examination, especially in those with concomitant risk factors for atherosclerosis, but we do not currently treat with empiric aspirin and/or rivaroxaban given their clinical equipoise in individuals with asymptomatic and stable peripheral arterial disease. Although individuals with CHIP have higher coronary artery calcium scores than those without CHIP, in asymptomatic patients we do not routinely screen for subclinical disease or perform ischemia testing unless clinically indicated, although we are more aggressive with lipid and blood pressure targets in individuals with TET2 or JAK2 CHIP and concomitant radiographic atherosclerotic disease (“particularly high risk” in Figure 2). We screen all patients with CHIP for arrhythmia and heart failure through a comprehensive history and physical examination, and we do not routinely advise laboratory or imaging testing in the absence of corresponding signs or symptoms.

We consider individuals with non-TET2, non-JAK2, and non-TP53/PPM1D CHIP, including DNMT3A CHIP, to have cardiovascular risk that is not clearly elevated beyond that of the general population on the basis of current evidence.

## Case Continued

We recommended the addition of ezetimibe 10 mg/d to achieve LDL-C <70 mg/dL. In the setting of hypertension, prior deep venous thrombosis, and TET2 CHIP, we advised the patient to continue low-dose daily aspirin. We also discussed vitamin C supplementation.

## Conclusions

In the coming decades, cardiovascular clinicians will be challenged with ameliorating the cardiovascular disease burden attributable to CHIP as the population continues to age and sequencing becomes more commonplace. Ongoing clinical trials—investigating an NLRP3 inflammasome inhibitor in patients with coronary artery disease and TET2 CHIP (GC43343) and a bispecific IL-1β and IL-18 inhibitor in patients with coronary artery disease and TET2 or DNMT3A CHIP (NCT06097663)—represent an exciting opportunity. However, outcome trials and U.S. Food and Drug Administration approval of CHIP-directed pharmacotherapies will not be immediate. In addition, although genome-editing technologies hold great promise for the design of CHIP therapeutics, multiple technological obstacles, including difficulties with tissue delivery and off-target effects, require consideration. In the meantime, we use existing science to inform risk stratification and use the available armamentarium of cardioprotection. Fundamentally, we practice intensive preventive cardiology pending clinical trial evidence regarding targeted therapies.

# Incorporating Management of Clonal Hematopoiesis of Indeterminant Potential (CHIP) into Cardiovascular Practice

**Authors:** Ohad Oren; Peter Libby

**Affiliations:** 1Cardiology Division, Massachusetts General Hospital, Boston, MA. | 2Cardiovascular Division, Brigham and Women’s Hospital, Harvard Medical School, Boston, MA.

Clonal hematopoiesis of indeterminate potential (CHIP) has emerged as a novel, common in older individuals, and potent risk factor for cardiovascular events (1). CHIP is defined as the presence of somatic mutations in hematopoietic stem cells with a variant allele frequency (VAF) of at least 2%, which corresponds to clones of myeloid cells comprising ≥4% of circulating blood leukocytes in the case of heterozygous mutations. CHIP was elucidated as pre-leukemic state but has been established as causal in the development of atherosclerotic and other cardiovascular diseases (2). Yet, despite great strides in understanding its biology, CHIP has not entered contemporary cardiovascular risk assessment. We argue that as genomic sequencing becomes more widespread, the cardiovascular community should prepare proactively and establish structures to evaluate and manage the growing number of individuals who will inevitably present with CHIP.

Seminal investigations over the past decade have demonstrated the biologic and clinical intersections between forms of CHIP, inflammation, and atherothrombosis. In addition, they have shown that the cardiovascular effects of CHIP vary depending on the mutated gene. TET2 and JAK2 CHIP involve heightened inflammation through activation of the NLRP3 and AIM2 inflammasomes, respectively (3,4). The resultant increase in IL-1β and IL-18 signaling boosts systemic inflammation and accelerates atherogenesis. JAK2 CHIP, beyond predisposing to arterial events, also elevates the risk of venous thrombosis through promotion of neutrophil extracellular trap (NET) formation. CHIP driven by mutations in DNA Damage Repair (DDR) genes, including TP53 and PPM1D, associates experimentally with lesional macrophage proliferation and incident peripheral arterial disease (5). CHIP also associates with heart failure and arrhythmias (notably atrial) among a growing number of other diseases.

To address the cardiovascular public health burden attributable to CHIP, we should develop dedicated cardiovascular clinics (Figure 1). These clinics, currently available in only a handful of centers, would provide a multidisciplinary platform for the individualized evaluation and care of persons with CHIP. In the absence of randomized trials supporting the benefits of diagnostic testing for cardiovascular assessment, we do not currently advocate screening of unselected populations. Instead, our proposed model aims to address the unmet need of patients referred from hematology and medical oncology providers for CHIP discovered during evaluation for new blood count abnormality, cancer predisposition, or cancer surveillance. Under that framework, patients with a new CHIP diagnosis would be evaluated by the CHIP cardiovascular specialist. Individuals classified as high risk (e.g., TET2, JAK2, DDR) may merit longitudinal management. The recognition of various forms of CHIP could inform a personalized approach to cardiovascular risk reduction. For example, an individual with large (>10% VAF) TET2 CHIP and borderline 10-year ASCVD risk would be counseled regarding aggressive risk reduction with intensification of lifestyle modifications and aggressive lipid-lowering and anti-hypertensive therapies. A patient with history of venous thrombosis and JAK2 clonal hematopoiesis warrants consideration of aspirin and lipid-lowering treatment. An individual with DNMT3A CHIP and a low 10-year ASCVD risk, however, does not merit such interventions. While there are currently no randomized clinical trials specifically supporting these interventions on the basis of CHIP status, our approach relies on shared decision-making to carefully balance potential benefits and risks. As with other preventive measures such as physical activity, which are widely recommended despite limited trial evidence in specific clinical settings, we implement treatments with well-established safety profiles and proven cardiovascular benefit in broader populations. We remain vigilant about drug-drug interactions and individual patient factors to minimize harm. Until CHIP-targeted therapies become available, this personalized strategy aims to reduce cardiovascular risk prudently without compromising patient safety.

To build and support CHIP cardiovascular clinics, health systems should designate “CHIP champions”, hematology, oncology, medical genetics, and cardiovascular specialists who devote a portion of their clinical and academic efforts to CHIP. Collaboration between such a multidisciplinary CHIP team would ensure coordinated care and best practices. In addition, including CHIP in training curricula would be desirable in general cardiovascular fellowships and in continuing medical education for practitioners. That effort would entail the development of a CHIP-focused curriculum that encompasses understanding of hematopoiesis and aspects of the biology of inflammation, genetics, and aging relevant to CHIP.

Successful implementation of this proposed framework for CHIP cardiovascular clinics requires overcoming several challenges. First, health insurance limitations often preclude patients from accessing and undergoing genomic sequencing studies and thus being identified with CHIP, for example when seeking causes for otherwise unexplained cardiovascular events. This concern has particular relevance in community medical sites, with limited availability of sequencing assays. Furthermore, CHIP cardiology visits could impose additional financial burden, particularly on uninsured patients and those facing high out-of-pocket expenditures, challenges that disproportionally affect racial and ethnic minority groups. Implementing effective policy and regulatory strategies, including streamlining prior authorization processes and expanding financial assistance programs, would help ensure equitable access to CHIP cardiovascular care for all.

The prospect of novel CHIP-targeted therapies highlights the growing importance of specialized CHIP cardiovascular clinics. The next few years are likely to equip the cardiovascular clinician with CHIP-targeted therapies aiming towards biologically-driven and personalized treatment pathways. Ongoing efficacy trials include inflammasome inhibitors – NLRP3 inhibitors in patients with coronary artery disease and elevated inflammatory markers and a bispecific IL-1β/IL-18 inhibitor in patients with coronary artery disease and TET2 or DNMT3A CHIP. Other promising avenues of investigation involve CHIP mutation-specific inhibitors and antagonists of biologic mediators downstream to the inflammasome. Advances in genome-editing technologies, such as CRISPR, are poised to accelerate the development of these targeted therapies by enabling precise correction of pathogenic mutations. Many clinical trials are now performing or planning CHIP ascertainment in participants that may inform precision allocation of therapies based on CHIP status.

Even before CHIP-targeted therapies are ready for prime time, the cardiovascular community can prepare proactively. With increasing availability of highly accurate genomic sequencing and the growing understanding of CHIP and its cardiovascular implications, institutions should develop standardized mechanisms to evaluate patients with CHIP systematically. Establishing infrastructures for formal education within medical training curricula could contribute to cultivating and sustaining a well-equipped CHIP cardiovascular workforce. CHIP constitutes an opportunity for our specialty and our patients.
